justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, anchored by whatever the prevailing price or level was at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 74.5 was driven primarily by short-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major catalysts were imminent. The one-week estimate of 75.2 incorporates a slight positive drift consistent with recent trend, while the one-month estimate of 76.5 reflects a continuation of that trend but tempered by the expectation that markets or the underlying variable tend to oscillate rather than move linearly. The gradual stepwise increase across horizons suggests I was pricing in mild bullish momentum without overcommitting to a strong directional view.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 3 points reflects typical intraday or overnight volatility. By one week, that range widens to about 12.5 points total, incorporating the possibility of a meaningful trend shift or a single large-move event. By one month, the interval spans 27 points, reflecting the genuine difficulty of predicting outcomes over a multi-week period when macro conditions, sentiment shifts, and structural factors can all evolve substantially.

The primary risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals are event-driven shocks that were not anticipated at the time of the forecast. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions, a policy surprise, or a liquidity-driven selloff could easily breach the lower bound of the one-month interval below 63. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — such as better-than-expected data, a policy pivot, or a short squeeze dynamic — could push the level above 90. These tail risks are real but were assigned low enough probability to fall outside the 90% confidence band by construction.

It is also worth noting that the confidence intervals assume a reasonably stable volatility regime. If realized volatility were to spike — for instance, due to geopolitical escalation or a financial contagion event — the true distribution of outcomes would have fatter tails than my stated intervals imply. Conversely, if conditions were unusually calm and range-bound, the actual outcomes might cluster much more tightly than even my one-day interval suggests. My intervals represent my best probabilistic judgment, not a guarantee that the true generating process matches my assumed model.
